context: Draw illustrations to bring out the anatomical difference between
solution:
Draw the transverse section (T.S.) of a sector of each root, side by side (book figure attached).

**Labels a marker looks for (both roots):** root hair, epidermis (epiblema), cortex, endodermis, pericycle, protoxylem, metaxylem, phloem, pith.

- **Dicot root (primary):** a wide cortex of thin-walled parenchyma; a single-layered endodermis; pericycle just inside it; a few (two to four) xylem patches alternating with phloem patches on different radii (radial arrangement), protoxylem towards the pericycle and metaxylem towards the centre; a **small or inconspicuous pith**.
- **Monocot root:** the same layers, but **many (more than six) xylem bundles** alternating with phloem patches around a **large, well developed pith**.

| Basis of difference | Dicot root | Monocot root |
|---|---|---|
| Number of xylem bundles | Usually two to four | Usually more than six (**polyarch**) |
| Pith | Small or inconspicuous | Large and well developed |
| Secondary growth | Occurs: a **cambium ring** develops later between xylem and phloem | Does not occur |

Common to both: epiblema with unicellular root hairs; cortex of thin-walled parenchyma with intercellular spaces; endodermis of barrel-shaped cells with **casparian strips** of suberin; pericycle; **radial** vascular bundles with parenchymatous **conjunctive tissue** between xylem and phloem (the book prints 'conjuctive tissue').

Book figure attached: (a) T.S. of dicot root, (b) T.S. of monocot root.
groundedIn: §6.2.1; §6.2.2; §6.1.3; Fig. 6.3 — dicot root epiblema, cortex, endodermis with casparian strips, pericycle, conjunctive tissue, two to four xylem and phloem patches, small pith, cambium ring develops later; monocot root polyarch, large pith, no secondary growth; radial arrangement in roots

context: Draw illustrations to bring out the anatomical difference between
solution:
Draw the transverse section (T.S.) of each stem as a whole outline plus an enlarged sector (book figure attached).

- **Dicot stem:** outline shows epidermis with epidermal hairs, hypodermis, cortex, endodermis, pericycle and a **ring of vascular bundles** separated by **medullary rays**, around a central **pith**. The sector is labelled epidermis, collenchyma (hypodermis), parenchyma, endodermis, pericycle (sclerenchyma patch above the phloem), phloem, cambium, metaxylem, protoxylem and pith.
- **Monocot stem:** outline shows epidermis, hypodermis and **many scattered vascular bundles** in a large **ground tissue**, smaller ones towards the periphery. The sector is labelled epidermis, hypodermis, vascular bundles (phloem, xylem) and ground tissue.

| Basis of difference | Dicot stem | Monocot stem |
|---|---|---|
| Hypodermis | Collenchymatous | Sclerenchymatous |
| Arrangement of vascular bundles | In a **ring** | **Scattered** |
| Type of vascular bundle | Conjoint, **open** (cambium present), endarch protoxylem | Conjoint, **closed** (no cambium) |
| Sclerenchyma around bundles | Semi-lunar patches of pericycle above the phloem | Each bundle surrounded by a sclerenchymatous **bundle sheath** |
| Ground tissue | Differentiated into cortex (with endodermis or starch sheath), pericycle, medullary rays and pith | A large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue |
| Phloem parenchyma | Present | Absent; water-containing cavities in the bundles |
| Size of bundles | Arranged in one ring | Peripheral bundles generally smaller than the centrally located ones |

Book figure attached: (a) T.S. of dicot stem, (b) T.S. of monocot stem.
groundedIn: §6.2.3; §6.2.4; §6.1.3; Fig. 6.4 — dicot stem collenchymatous hypodermis, endodermis as starch sheath, semi-lunar sclerenchyma pericycle, medullary rays, ring of conjoint open endarch bundles, pith; monocot stem sclerenchymatous hypodermis, scattered conjoint closed bundles with sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, large ground tissue, phloem parenchyma absent, water-containing cavities; BEYOND CHAPTER: phloem parenchyma present in the dicot stem

stem: Cut a transverse section of young stem of a plant from your school garden and observe it under the microscope. How would you ascertain whether it is a monocot stem or a dicot stem? Give reasons.
solution:
The stem is identified mainly by the **arrangement and type of its vascular bundles**, supported by the hypodermis and ground tissue.

| Basis | If dicot stem | If monocot stem |
|---|---|---|
| Vascular bundles | Arranged in a **ring** | **Scattered** in the ground tissue |
| Type of bundle | Conjoint and **open**: cambium between phloem and xylem; endarch protoxylem | Conjoint and **closed**: no cambium |
| Bundle sheath | No sheath around each bundle; semi-lunar sclerenchyma patches (pericycle) above the phloem | Each bundle surrounded by a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath** |
| Hypodermis | Few layers of **collenchyma** | **Sclerenchymatous** |
| Ground tissue | Cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle, **medullary rays** and a central **pith** | Large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue |
| Inside the bundle | Phloem parenchyma present | Phloem parenchyma absent; water-containing cavities present |

**Reasons:**
1. The **ring arrangement** of vascular bundles is a characteristic of the dicot stem.
2. Presence of **cambium** makes the bundles open, able to form secondary xylem and phloem; monocot bundles lack cambium and are closed.
3. Scattered bundles with sclerenchymatous sheaths, a sclerenchymatous hypodermis and absence of phloem parenchyma are features of the monocot stem.
groundedIn: §6.2.3; §6.2.4; §6.1.3; Fig. 6.4 — ring arrangement of bundles a characteristic of dicot stem; conjoint open endarch bundles; collenchymatous hypodermis, starch sheath, medullary rays, pith; monocot scattered conjoint closed bundles with sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, sclerenchymatous hypodermis, phloem parenchyma absent, water-containing cavities; cambium makes bundles open; BEYOND CHAPTER: phloem parenchyma present in the dicot stem

stem: The transverse section of a plant material shows the following anatomical features - (a) the vascular bundles are conjoint, scattered and surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheaths. (b) phloem parenchyma is absent. What will you identify it as?
solution:
It is a **monocot stem** (T.S. of a monocotyledonous stem).

Reasons:
1. **Scattered** vascular bundles, each surrounded by a **sclerenchymatous bundle sheath**, are characteristic of the monocot stem (a dicot stem has its bundles in a ring).
2. The bundles are **conjoint**, which occurs in stems and leaves, not in roots (roots have radial bundles).
3. **Phloem parenchyma is absent** in the monocot stem.
groundedIn: §6.2.4; §6.1.3; §6.2.3 — monocot stem has scattered vascular bundles each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, conjoint and closed, phloem parenchyma absent; conjoint bundles common in stems and leaves, radial in roots; ring arrangement characteristic of dicot stem

stem: What is stomatal apparatus? Explain the structure of stomata with a labelled diagram.
solution:
**Stomatal apparatus:** the stomatal aperture, the guard cells and the surrounding subsidiary cells are together called the stomatal apparatus.

**Structure of stomata:**
1. **Stomata** are structures present in the **epidermis of leaves**; they regulate **transpiration and gaseous exchange**.
2. Each stoma is composed of two **bean-shaped guard cells** which enclose the **stomatal pore**. In **grasses**, the guard cells are **dumb-bell shaped**.
3. The **outer walls** of the guard cells (away from the pore) are **thin**, and the **inner walls** (towards the pore) are **highly thickened**.
4. The guard cells possess **chloroplasts** and regulate the opening and closing of stomata.
5. A few epidermal cells in the vicinity of the guard cells become specialised in shape and size; these are the **subsidiary cells**.

**Diagram** (book figure attached): (a) a stoma with bean-shaped guard cells and (b) a stoma with dumb-bell shaped guard cells, labelled **epidermal cells, subsidiary cells, guard cells, chloroplast** and **stomatal pore**.
groundedIn: §6.1.1; Fig. 6.1 — stomata in the epidermis of leaves regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange; two bean-shaped guard cells enclose the stomatal pore, dumb-bell shaped in grasses; outer walls thin, inner walls highly thickened; chloroplasts; subsidiary cells; stomatal apparatus

stem: Name the three basic tissue systems in the flowering plants. Give the tissue names under each system.
solution:
On the basis of structure and location, the three tissue systems are the **epidermal tissue system**, the **ground (fundamental) tissue system** and the **vascular (conducting) tissue system**.

1. **Epidermal tissue system:** the outermost covering of the plant body. It comprises **epidermal cells** (parenchymatous, usually single-layered, often covered by a **cuticle**), **stomata** (guard cells and subsidiary cells) and **epidermal appendages**: root hairs and trichomes.
2. **Ground tissue system:** all tissues except epidermis and vascular bundles. It consists of the simple tissues **parenchyma, collenchyma** and **sclerenchyma**, forming the cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays in primary stems and roots, and the **mesophyll** in leaves.
3. **Vascular tissue system:** the complex tissues **xylem** and **phloem**, which together form the vascular bundles; in dicot stems **cambium** is present between them.
groundedIn: §6.1; §6.1.1; §6.1.2; §6.1.3 — three tissue systems on the basis of structure and location; epidermal cells, stomata, cuticle, trichomes and hairs; ground tissue of parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma in cortex, pericycle, pith, medullary rays, mesophyll in leaves; xylem and phloem form vascular bundles, cambium in dicot stems

stem: How is the study of plant anatomy useful to us?
solution:
**Plant anatomy**, the study of the internal structure of plants, is useful in the following ways:

1. **Understanding function:** it shows how cells are organised into tissues and tissues into organs, and how structure suits function, e.g. root hairs absorb water and minerals, stomata regulate transpiration and gaseous exchange, and xylem and phloem conduct water, minerals and food.
2. **Identification and classification:** monocots and dicots are anatomically different (number and arrangement of vascular bundles, open or closed bundles, size of pith), so anatomy helps identify and classify plants.
3. **Adaptations to environment:** internal structures show adaptations to diverse environments, e.g. the cuticle and trichomes reduce water loss, and **bulliform cells** of grasses curl the leaf inwards under water stress.
4. **Secondary growth:** the presence of cambium shows which plants (most dicot roots and stems) can grow in thickness.
5. **Economic uses:** it helps identify **timber and fibre** and judge their quality, and detect **adulteration** in plant-based drugs by their tissue features.
6. **Crop improvement:** plant breeders use anatomical features to select varieties suited to particular conditions.
groundedIn: §6.0; §6.1.1; §6.1.3; §6.2.2; §6.2.6 — anatomy is the study of internal structure; cells into tissues into organs; monocots and dicots anatomically different; adaptations to diverse environments; cuticle, trichomes, stomata, root hairs; bulliform cells; open bundles form secondary tissues; BEYOND CHAPTER: identifying timber and fibre and judging their quality, detecting adulteration in plant-based drugs, use by plant breeders to select varieties

stem: Describe the internal structure of a dorsiventral leaf with the help of labelled diagrams.
solution:
A vertical section of a **dorsiventral (dicot) leaf** through the lamina shows three main parts: **epidermis, mesophyll** and **vascular system**.

1. **Epidermis:** covers the upper surface (**adaxial epidermis**) and the lower surface (**abaxial epidermis**); both have a conspicuous **cuticle**. The abaxial epidermis generally bears **more stomata**; the adaxial epidermis may even lack them. Each stoma opens into a **sub-stomatal cavity**.
2. **Mesophyll:** the tissue between the two epidermises, made of parenchyma with chloroplasts, which carries out photosynthesis. It has two types of cells:
   - **Palisade parenchyma:** adaxially placed, elongated cells arranged vertically and parallel to each other.
   - **Spongy parenchyma:** oval or round, loosely arranged cells below the palisade, extending to the lower epidermis, with numerous large spaces and **air cavities**.
3. **Vascular system:** vascular bundles in the veins and midrib; their size depends on the size of the veins, which vary in thickness in the **reticulate venation** of dicot leaves. Each bundle is conjoint, with **xylem towards the adaxial side** and phloem towards the abaxial side, and is surrounded by a layer of thick-walled **bundle sheath** cells.

**Diagram** (book figure attached): T.S. of dicot leaf labelled **adaxial epidermis, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, air cavity, sub-stomatal cavity, stoma, abaxial epidermis, bundle sheath, xylem** and **phloem**.
groundedIn: §6.2.5; §6.1.3; Fig. 6.5 — vertical section shows epidermis, mesophyll and vascular system; adaxial and abaxial epidermis with conspicuous cuticle, abaxial bears more stomata; palisade and spongy parenchyma, air cavities; vascular bundles in veins and midrib, reticulate venation, thick-walled bundle sheath; conjoint bundles in leaves; sub-stomatal cavity labelled in the figure; BEYOND CHAPTER: xylem towards the adaxial side and phloem towards the abaxial side of the leaf bundle
